meta.subtitle: A $20 billion quarter and data-center power demand against a full 35.0x trailing multiple and thinner free cash flow

advisories: model vs Street expected return diverge by 57pp — informational, not scored

analystSentiment.commentary: We rate Caterpillar HOLD with an $860 to $930 target range against a current price of $812.02. The operating case is strong: second-quarter 2026 sales and revenues reached $20.543 billion, {+ up 24 percent +} from $16.569 billion a year earlier, and operating profit margin widened to 20.9 percent from 17.3 percent. Consensus places FY26E revenue near $79.2 billion. The restraint is price and cash: the shares trade at 35.0x trailing earnings, and cash conversion thinned in FY25, so the stock has little cash support at this level. Our probability-weighted fair value sits modestly above the current price, for an expected upside of 9.0 percent against a bear-case downside of 23.0 percent. That derives HOLD. The call is close, both BUY tests fall short, and the deciding judgment is the multiple we assume for the Base case.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Caterpillar Inc. manufactures construction and mining equipment, off-highway diesel and natural gas engines, industrial gas turbines, and diesel-electric locomotives, selling in the United States and internationally. Its three primary segments are Construction Industries, Resource Industries, and Power & Energy, alongside a Financial Products segment and an All Other segment. Financial Products provides operating and finance leases, installment sale contracts, wholesale financing, and insurance, so consolidated revenue and debt include a captive-finance business. The company was incorporated in 1925 and is headquartered in Irving, Texas. The vendor treats Caterpillar as a single consolidated segment, with FY25 revenue of $67.6 billion; the segment detail in this report is drawn from the filing's own disclosures.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: Caterpillar is in a synchronized upcycle, with second-quarter 2026 sales higher across all three primary segments and data-center demand lifting its power business. Sales and revenues {+ rose 24 percent +} to $20.543 billion, driven by $3.1 billion of higher sales volume and $595 million of favorable price realization. Separately, quarterly profit {+ rose 65 percent +} to $3.593 billion, which the MD&A attributes mainly to the profit impact of higher sales volume. The bull case is that this demand persists through 2026 and 2027 as the company expands capacity. The bear case is that the shares already discount much of it at a full trailing multiple, and a cyclical downturn in mining or construction would cut earnings and the multiple at once.

catalysts: Data-center power demand: management anticipates continued growth in reciprocating engines and turbines for power generation to support cloud-computing and generative-AI build-out.
Full-year 2026 guidance: management now anticipates sales and revenues growth in the mid-to-high teens for 2026 versus 2025, with strong growth expected across each primary segment.
IEEPA refunds: further refund claims, still under assessment, could add to the recovery already booked in the second quarter of 2026.
Third-quarter 2026 outlook: management anticipates strong sales and revenues growth versus the third quarter of 2025, with higher sales volume and favorable price realization in each primary segment.

Construction spending: the MD&A expects Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act funds to support construction spending over the next few years; the quarter's 50 percent rise in Construction Industries' North America sales came from higher sales to end users and changes in dealer inventories.
risks: Cyclicality: the 2025 Form 10-K says demand tends to be cyclical; the risks section sets out the mechanism.
Valuation: the shares trade at a full multiple on both trailing and forward earnings, leaving little room for disappointment.
Cash conversion: shareholder returns ran ahead of free cash flow in FY24 and FY25, as the capital-allocation discussion details.
Tariffs: 2026 tariff costs remain large, as the risks section details.
Commodity dependence: Resource Industries' 2026 outlook rests primarily on rising demand for copper and gold.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Full-year 2025 revenue was $67.6 billion, up 4.3 percent, but operating income fell to $11.2 billion and operating margin {- narrowed to 16.5 percent from 20.2 percent -} in FY24, while diluted EPS declined to $18.81 from $22.05. 2026 has reversed that. The quarter's revenue jump carried into profitability: operating profit reached $4.295 billion, {+ up 50 percent +}, and operating profit margin recovered to 20.9 percent from 17.3 percent. Quarterly profit per share was $7.77, up from $4.62, and adjusted profit per share was $8.17. For the six months ended June 30, 2026, sales were $37.958 billion, up 23 percent, and profit per share was $13.23 versus $8.82. Operating profit in the quarter included $392 million of expected IEEPA tariff recoveries, which flatters the year-over-year comparison.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: Caterpillar ended FY25 with $10.0 billion of cash and short-term investments, total debt of $36.2 billion, and net debt of $26.2 billion, up from $24.9 billion in FY24, against total equity of $21.3 billion. Total debt rose from $31.7 billion in FY24, and the current ratio was 1.44 at year-end and 1.37 on a trailing-twelve-month basis. Debt looks heavy against equity, but consolidated debt includes Financial Products, the captive-finance arm; our sources do not split borrowings between that lending book and the industrial business, so consolidated leverage may overstate the industrial balance sheet by an amount the data shown does not quantify. Credit quality at the finance arm is stable: past dues at Cat Financial were 1.31 percent at the end of the second quarter of 2026 versus 1.62 percent a year earlier, and the allowance for credit losses was $294 million, or 0.84 percent of finance receivables. The company ended the quarter with $6.7 billion of enterprise cash.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Operating cash flow was $11.7 billion in FY25, down from $12.0 billion in FY24, while capital expenditure rose to $4.3 billion from $3.2 billion. Free cash flow therefore {- fell to $7.5 billion from $8.8 billion -}, and FCF margin narrowed to 11.0 percent from 13.6 percent. Most of that decline came from higher capital spending rather than from the small dip in operating cash flow, and capital expenditure has risen in every year shown since FY21. Management guides to capital expenditures of approximately $3.5 billion in 2026, which is below the FY25 figure in the data shown; our sources do not reconcile the two, so we do not read the guide as a cut in spending. FY25 share repurchases were $5.2 billion and dividends $2.7 billion. In the second quarter of 2026 the company deployed $1.5 billion on repurchases and $0.7 billion on dividends, and enterprise operating cash flow was $6.2 billion for the six months ended June 30, 2026. The dividend yields 0.81 percent at the current price, so the return of capital comes mostly through buybacks.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: At $812.02 the shares trade at 35.0x trailing earnings, 5.0x sales, 25.8x trailing EV/EBITDA, and 29.9x the vendor's next-twelve-month earnings. That multiple matches the current price over the FY26E consensus EPS of $27.19, so we treat it as a current-year multiple; on FY27E EPS of $32.38 the multiple is about 25.1x. The trailing multiple is full for a company whose earnings are cyclical and fell in FY25, and a trailing FCF yield of 2.4 percent gives the price little cash support. No peer multiples were provided, so the comparison here is against Caterpillar's own forward estimates rather than a peer set. Market capitalization is about $373.3 billion on roughly 459.67 million shares. The shares sit well below the 52-week high of $1,073.46, and none of our sources explains the decline from that high. Consensus sits at a $975.61 target, up 20.1 percent, with a median of $980.50 and a range of $575.00 to $1,225.00; the 28 analysts split 14 Buy, 12 Hold, and 2 Sell for a Buy consensus.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: The demand drivers in the growth section stay strong through 2027, margins hold near the second quarter's 20.9 percent, and estimates keep rising. We value FY27E EPS of $32.38 at about 33x, above today's current-year multiple, on the basis that the market pays more for growth it sees extending past 2027. That returns the shares to around the 52-week high of $1,073.46.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: The upcycle continues but decelerates: full-year 2026 revenue lands near the $79.2 billion consensus, and FY27E revenue reaches $88.1 billion with EPS at the FY27E consensus. A year out FY27 is the current year, and we value it at about 28x, a step below today's current-year multiple, on the basis that revenue growth slows from the 2026 pace and the shares are then priced later in the cycle, as the scenario commentary argues.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Demand peaks in 2027: volume growth stops as dealers work down the Construction Industries inventory management expects to be higher at year-end 2026, cost increases like those guided for 2026 continue, and the quarter's one-off IEEPA recovery does not recur. FY27 earnings stall near the FY26E consensus of $27.19. We value that at about 23x, a sharp step down from today's 29.9x current-year multiple, because that multiple pays for growth a stall removes; we stop short of a deeper cut because earnings hold rather than fall.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the Base case at 45 percent, the Bull at 30 percent, and the Bear at 25 percent. The Bull carries more weight than the Bear because management reports strong order rates and a growing backlog across all three primary segments, though without figures; the Bear keeps a quarter of the weight because the 2025 Form 10-K says demand tends to be cyclical, and the cycle, not the franchise, sets the earnings level. All three cases value a year-out current-year EPS, so their multiples compare directly with today's current-year multiple. The weights produce a probability-weighted fair value modestly above the current price, an expected upside of 9.0 percent, a bear-case downside of 23.0 percent, and a reward/risk of 0.39 times, which derives HOLD: both BUY tests fall short, and reward/risk falls further short than expected upside. The call is close, and the deciding judgment is the Base multiple. The case for holding today's multiple a year out is real: FY27E EPS grows faster than FY27E revenue, so consensus expects margins to keep widening; the price that multiple implies sits near the Street's consensus and median targets; and the order and backlog claims point to demand beyond 2026. The case for a step down is that FY27E revenue growth is slower than FY26E's +17 percent, so a year out the shares will be priced later in the cycle; our sources hold no peer or history to show today's multiple is a normal level for Caterpillar; and the thin FCF yield gives it little cash support. We think the step down is the more likely outcome, though not by a wide margin, and use about 28x; holding today's multiple would derive BUY. A rollover that takes earnings back toward FY25's $18.81 would be a tail outside the Bear, not a reason to raise its weight. Our $860 to $930 target range brackets the Base case.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Caterpillar is one consolidated group for the vendor, but the filing reports primary segments. In the second quarter of 2026, Construction Industries sales were $8.346 billion, up 35 percent; Power & Energy sales were $8.238 billion, up 17 percent, with Power Generation up 29 percent on data-center demand for reciprocating engines and turbines; and Resource Industries sales were $4.648 billion, up 20 percent, tied to mining and commodity demand. Financial Products, the captive-finance arm, rounds out the group. The mix spreads Caterpillar across construction, energy, mining, and financing, which diversifies end-market exposure but leaves the whole group geared to the industrial and commodity cycle.

moatFactors.name: Global dealer network
moatFactors.body: Caterpillar sells and services through an independent dealer network worldwide; the MD&A tracks dealer inventories and dealer rental fleet loading as demand signals, underscoring how central dealers are to distribution and customer relationships.

moatFactors.name: Aftermarket parts and services
moatFactors.body: Recurring parts, rebuild, and services revenue accompany the installed base, and Resource Industries includes wear and maintenance components and fleet-management technology; the services outlook is covered in the growth section.

moatFactors.name: Scale and breadth
moatFactors.body: The company spans construction, mining, energy, transportation, and financing, with $67.6 billion of FY25 revenue across the segments described above, giving it manufacturing scale and a product range that reaches many end markets.

moatFactors.name: Captive financing
moatFactors.body: Financial Products offers leases, installment contracts, and wholesale financing that support equipment sales; segment revenues were $1.145 billion in the second quarter of 2026, up 10 percent, with credit quality stable.

businessMoat.durability: The competitive position is durable but the earnings are cyclical. The dealer network, aftermarket revenue, and scale are hard to replicate and persist across cycles, which supports a wide-moat view. What the moat does not do is smooth the cycle: the FY25 margin slip shown in the income-statement discussion came even as revenue grew, and the 2025 Form 10-K warns that the business and the industries it serves are highly sensitive to global and regional economic conditions. The current strength is a cyclical high rather than a new baseline, so the durability of the franchise should not be confused with durability of the current earnings level.

points: Power & Energy's growth reaches beyond data centers: Oil and Gas sales rose 9 percent in the second quarter of 2026 on reciprocating engines for gas compression and turbine-related services, and management expects Oil & Gas to grow moderately in 2026.

Resource Industries has its own driver: management expects end-user equipment sales to rise in 2026, primarily on rising demand for copper and gold, and reports robust order rates and strong backlog growth in the segment.
Rail adds a further leg: Rail sales rose 15 percent in the quarter on higher international locomotive deliveries, and management expects rail services and locomotive deliveries to grow in 2026.

Aftermarket growth: management expects services revenues to grow in 2026 and rebuild activity to increase moderately, which adds revenue tied to the installed base rather than to new-equipment orders alone.
Consensus models FY26E revenue of about $79.2 billion and FY27E of $88.1 billion, with EPS rising from $27.19 to $32.38, faster than revenue.

management.leadership: Joe Creed is Chairman and CEO. In the August 4, 2026 earnings release he called the quarter's more than $20 billion in sales and revenues a milestone in company history, and pointed to strong order rates and a growing backlog across all three primary segments. Neither the order rates nor the backlog is quantified in our sources, so the weight this report gives the Bull over the Bear rests partly on management's word.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation leans on buybacks over dividends, and the payout has run ahead of free cash flow: FY25 repurchases and dividends together exceeded the year's free cash flow, as they did in FY24, and net debt rose in FY25, as the balance-sheet discussion shows. The payout has therefore not been covered by free cash flow alone, and capital spending now absorbs a larger share of operating cash flow than it did in FY23. The dividend is small relative to buybacks, so most of the return flexes with repurchases; in a downturn management can throttle them quickly, which protects the balance sheet but means the shareholder return is not a floor. We would not treat the current buyback pace as a steady return, because it depends on the cycle and on how much the company reinvests.
management.governance: Governance rests on the 2026 proxy statement. The board's guidelines cap non-independent directors at two, and for 2025 the board determined every director independent except Mr. Umpleby and Mr. Creed. Related-party transactions expected to exceed $120,000 in a calendar year must be approved in advance by the NGC. The proxy discloses two family-employment matters: Mr. Creed's brother-in-law received $183,089 under a separation agreement after his employment ceased in February 2025, and Mr. Jason Kaiser's brother-in-law, a manager in product support, earned about $210,000 in fiscal 2025 in line with employees of similar title. Both are disclosed in the proxy's related-party section, and both amounts are small relative to the company.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy excerpt in our sources covers director independence and related-party transactions but does not quantify insider or institutional ownership, so no ownership figure is stated here.

idiosyncratic: Tariffs are a moving target. The company expects around $2.2 billion of 2026 tariff costs and about $600 million in the third quarter of 2026. It recorded $392 million of expected IEEPA tariff recoveries after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled those tariffs unauthorized on February 20, 2026, but additional recoveries are not assured and were not deemed probable as of June 30, 2026.

Dealer inventory swings distort reported sales. Management expects an unfavorable impact from changes in Construction Industries dealer inventories in the second half of 2026, including a more typical decrease of over $1.0 billion in the fourth quarter, which will weigh on reported volume versus the prior year.

Cost inflation is set to eat into the flow-through. For the third quarter and full-year 2026, management expects the profit impact of higher volume and price to be partially offset by unfavorable manufacturing costs and higher SG&A and R&D expenses. We expect revenue to convert to profit less efficiently than in the second quarter, which also carried the one-off IEEPA recovery.
Margin fragility is real: the FY25 operating-margin decline noted in the income-statement discussion came in a year of revenue growth, so revenue growth alone does not protect margins.
risks.systemic: The systemic risk is the cycle. Caterpillar's 2025 Form 10-K states that demand for its products and services tends to be cyclical and can be significantly reduced in periods of economic weakness, lower government and business investment, tighter credit conditions, or perceived or actual industry overcapacity. Customers in energy, transportation, and mining are likely to base their purchase decisions on expected future commodity dynamics, including price, and the rates of infrastructure spending, commercial construction, and housing starts also play a significant role. A synchronized slowdown across these end markets would cut volume and pricing at once, and the full trailing multiple would likely compress alongside earnings. The Financial Products book adds credit risk in a downturn, though Cat Financial's past dues were lower than a year earlier.

body: Caterpillar earns a HOLD, with the target range set at $860 to $930 while the shares trade at $812.02. The operating case is real: the second-quarter surge, sharply higher margins and earnings, and the full-year guidance set out above.

The restraint is price, the cycle, and thinner cash conversion. At a full multiple on both trailing and current-year earnings the shares price in much of the upcycle, and the 2025 Form 10-K says demand tends to be cyclical. The label rests on the current close as well as on the Base multiple: with the scenarios unchanged, a small fall in the share price would derive BUY, and SELL would derive at a price still below the $975.61 consensus target. We would re-run the analysis if FY27 consensus moves materially or if the third-quarter 2026 results put figures on the order and backlog claims.
